“Some time elapsed before I recovered enough composure to attend to the balloon’s ordinary needs. I then inspected it closely and, to my immense relief, discovered no damage. All my instruments were secure, and neither provisions nor ballast had been lost. Indeed, I had fastened them so firmly in place that such a mishap was impossible. My watch showed six o’clock. I continued to rise swiftly, and the barometer indicated a height of three and three-quarter miles. Directly below, upon the ocean, appeared a little black object, somewhat oblong, seemingly the size and very image of the childish plaything called a domino. Through my telescope I clearly recognized a British ship mounting ninety-four guns, sailing close to the wind and pitching heavily, her head pointed west-southwest. Apart from this vessel, nothing met my eyes but sea, sky, and the sun, which had risen long before.

“It is time, your Excellencies, that I explained the purpose of my dangerous journey. You will recall that my desperate circumstances in Rotterdam had finally determined me upon suicide. I felt no actual loathing for life itself; rather, the incidental sufferings of my situation had harassed me past endurance. Wishing to live, yet exhausted by living, I found in the treatise at the bookseller’s stall an opening for my imagination. My decision was at last complete. I would depart and nevertheless remain alive; abandon the world and still exist. To speak without riddles, I resolved, whatever the consequences, to make my way to the moon if I could. Lest you suppose me madder than I really am, I shall explain as fully as possible the arguments that persuaded me such an undertaking, though certainly difficult and undeniably hazardous, did not lie wholly beyond the reach of a courageous spirit.

“The first consideration was the moon’s true distance from the earth. The average separation between the centres of these two planets is 59.9643 terrestrial equatorial radii, or merely some 237,000 miles. I say the average separation, for it must be remembered that the moon follows an ellipse whose eccentricity amounts to no less than 0.05484 of its major semi-axis, with the earth’s centre placed at one focus. Thus, if I could somehow arrange to encounter the moon at perigee, as it were, the distance just stated would be considerably reduced.

“Mrs. Otis also tells me—and she has considerable authority on art, having enjoyed several winters in Boston as a girl—that these jewels are worth a great deal of money and would sell for a substantial price. Given that, Lord Canterville, I am sure you understand why I cannot allow any member of my family to keep them. Such vain ornaments and playthings, however appropriate or necessary to the dignity of the British aristocracy, would be entirely unsuitable for people raised on the strict and, I believe, immortal principles of republican simplicity. I should perhaps add that Virginia very much hopes you will let her retain the box as a keepsake of your unfortunate, though misguided, ancestor. Since it is extremely old and therefore rather dilapidated, you may feel able to grant her request. Personally, I am surprised that a child of mine should show sympathy for anything medieval. I can explain it only by remembering that Virginia was born in a London suburb shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from Athens.”

Lord Canterville listened to the worthy Minister with great seriousness, occasionally tugging his gray moustache to conceal an involuntary smile. When Mr. Otis finished, he shook his hand warmly. “My dear sir, your charming daughter did my unfortunate ancestor, Sir Simon, a very important service. My family and I owe her a great deal for her remarkable courage and spirit. The jewels are plainly hers. Indeed, if I were heartless enough to take them away, I believe that wicked old fellow would climb out of his grave within a fortnight and make my life hell. As for heirlooms, nothing is legally an heirloom unless a will or other document identifies it as such, and nobody knew these jewels existed. I assure you that I have no more right to them than your butler. When Miss Virginia grows up, I imagine she will enjoy having beautiful things to wear. Besides, Mr. Otis, you forget that you purchased both the furniture and the ghost at their assessed value. Everything the ghost owned therefore became yours at once. Whatever activity Sir Simon displayed in the corridor at night, he was legally dead, and you bought his property.”

Country people, butchers, cattle drivers, street sellers, boys, thieves, loafers, and vagabonds of every kind crowded together in a single mass. Drivers whistled, dogs barked, oxen bellowed and lunged, sheep bleated, and pigs grunted and squealed. Sellers called out over shouting, swearing, and arguments on every side. Bells rang and voices roared from every public house. People pushed, drove, struck, whooped, and yelled. The awful, clashing noise came from every corner of the market, while unwashed, unshaven, filthy figures ran constantly back and forth, bursting into and out of the crowd. It was a deafening, bewildering scene that overwhelmed the senses.

Dragging Oliver behind him, Mr. Sikes forced his way through the thickest crowd. He barely noticed the sights and sounds that astonished the boy. He nodded two or three times to acquaintances and refused as many invitations to take a morning drink. Without stopping, he pushed on until they escaped the uproar and went through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, youngster!” Sikes said, glancing at St. Andrew’s Church clock. “Nearly seven! You need to move faster. Come on, don’t start falling behind already, lazybones!”

He reinforced this instruction with a sharp pull on Oliver’s wrist. The boy quickened into something between a fast walk and a run, keeping up with the burglar’s long, rapid strides as well as he could.

They maintained this speed past Hyde Park Corner and toward Kensington. Then Sikes slowed until an empty cart coming from behind caught up. Seeing “Hounslow” painted on it, he asked the driver, as politely as he could manage, whether they might ride as far as Isleworth.

“Climb in,” the man said. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes, he’s mine,” Sikes answered, staring hard at Oliver and slipping a hand casually into the pocket containing his pistol.

“Your father walks a little too fast for you, doesn’t he, young fellow?” the driver asked, noticing Oliver’s breathlessness.

“Not at all,” Sikes interrupted. “He’s used to it. Here, Ned, take my hand. Up you get!”

Addressing Oliver this way, he helped him into the cart. The driver pointed to a pile of sacks and told him to lie there and rest.

As each milestone passed, Oliver wondered more anxiously where his companion intended to take him. They passed Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford, yet continued steadily onward as though the journey had only just begun.
